title: Longest Shared Leading Digits
statement:
You get two lists of positive integers, a and b. For a number x from a and a number y from b, their shared lead is the number of leading digits they have in common. For example, 1450 and 1459 share 145, a lead of 3, and 27 and 72 share nothing, a lead of 0.

Look at every pair with one number from each list (not just numbers at the same index). Return the longest shared lead over all pairs, or 0 if no pair shares even a first digit.

examples.why: 1450 and 145 share "145". The other pairs share less: 92 and 9301 share "9", 7 and 78 share "7".
Every number in a starts with 5 and every number in b starts with 6.
Pairs at the same index share nothing, but 2024 from a and 2025 from b share "202".

hints: Comparing every pair works but is 50 000 × 50 000 pairs. Can you store what one list offers so the other list can query it?
A number with d digits has only d leading prefixes. All prefixes of all numbers in a fit in a set or a trie.
Insert every number of a into a digit trie. For each number in b, walk down the trie digit by digit until there is no matching child. The depth reached is its best lead against all of a at once.

explain.intuition:
The shared lead of x and y is the length of the longest prefix of y that is also a prefix of x. So the question for each y becomes: what is the longest prefix of y that is a prefix of any number in a? That answers all pairs with y at once.

A trie of the digits of a answers this in one walk: follow y's digits from the root until a child is missing. A set of prefixes works too: put every prefix of every number of a into a set (at most 9 per number, since the values are below 10⁹), then cut digits off the end of y until the remainder is in the set. Both cost about 9 steps per number instead of one step per pair.
steps: Build an empty trie whose children are indexed by digit.
Insert each number of a as a digit string, creating nodes as needed.
For each number of b, start at the root and follow its digits while the matching child exists, counting the steps.
Keep the largest count seen and return it.
pitfalls: Comparing only a[i] with b[i]. The third example's best pair is at different indexes.

Sorting both lists and comparing neighbours by value. Numeric closeness isn't digit closeness: 1999 and 2000 differ by 1 but share no leading digit. If you sort, sort the digit strings, not the numbers.
Pairwise comparison passes on small inputs but does 2.5 · 10⁹ comparisons on the largest ones.

solutions.title: Compare every pair
solutions.idea: Turn each number into a string and count matching leading characters for all pairs.

solutions.title: Set of every prefix
solutions.idea: Store all numeric prefixes of a (x, x / 10, x / 100, …). For each y, drop its last digit until the value is in the set.

solutions.title: Digit trie
solutions.idea: Insert every number of a digit by digit. Walk each number of b down the trie; the depth reached is its best lead.

followups: Return the pair itself, not just the length. What extra data does each trie node need?
The lists are strings of letters, not numbers, and some are thousands of characters long. Does the trie still beat the prefix set, and why?
lcTitle: Find the Length of the Longest Common Prefix
